This is a **CMOS inverter** (logic NOT gate), the most fundamental building block of digital CMOS circuits.

| Device | Type | Source | Gate | Drain | Role |
|--------|------|--------|------|-------|------|
| **M₂** (top) | PMOS | V_DD | V_in | V_out | Pull-up |
| **M₁** (bottom) | NMOS | GND | V_in | V_out | Pull-down |

The two **gates are tied together** → input V_in
The two **drains are tied together** → output V_out

## Operating Principle

The two transistors operate in **complementary** fashion — one conducts while the other is off.

**Case 1: V_in = LOW (0 V)**
- NMOS M₁: $V_{GS} = 0 < V_{TH,n}$ → **OFF**
- PMOS M₂: $V_{GS} = -V_{DD} < V_{TH,p}$ → **ON**
- Output pulled up → **V_out = V_DD (HIGH)**

**Case 2: V_in = HIGH (V_DD)**
- NMOS M₁: $V_{GS} = V_{DD} > V_{TH,n}$ → **ON**
- PMOS M₂: $V_{GS} = 0$ → **OFF**
- Output pulled down → **V_out = 0 (LOW)**

$$\boxed{V_{out} = \overline{V_{in}}}$$

## Voltage Transfer Characteristic (VTC)

As V_in sweeps from 0 to V_DD, the inverter passes through **5 regions**:

```
Vout
 VDD |‾‾‾‾‾‾\
     |       \  (both in saturation
     |        | → steep transition)
     |         \
   0 |__________\______ Vin
     0    VM    VDD
```

| Region | V_in range | M₁ (NMOS) | M₂ (PMOS) |
|--------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| A | $< V_{TH,n}$ | OFF | triode |
| B | low–mid | saturation | triode |
| C | $\approx V_M$ | saturation | saturation |
| D | mid–high | triode | saturation |
| E | $> V_{DD}-\|V_{TH,p}\|$ | triode | OFF |

**Switching threshold** (where V_in = V_out):
$$V_M = \frac{V_{DD} - |V_{TH,p}| + V_{TH,n}\sqrt{k_n/k_p}}{1 + \sqrt{k_n/k_p}}, \qquad k = \mu C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}$$

For a **symmetric** design ($k_n = k_p$, $|V_{TH,p}| = V_{TH,n}$): $V_M = V_{DD}/2$.

## Key Properties

- ✅ **Zero static power** — one device is always off, so no DC current flows (except tiny leakage)
- ✅ **Full rail-to-rail swing** — output reaches exactly 0 and V_DD (high noise margins)
- ✅ **High input impedance** — gates draw essentially no DC current
- ⚡ **Dynamic power only** — power consumed mainly during switching: $P \approx f C_L V_{DD}^2$
- 📈 **High gain** in the transition region (both devices saturated) → sharp, well-defined logic transition

This circuit's efficiency (no static dissipation) is precisely why CMOS dominates modern integrated-circuit design.

# Circuit Analysis: CMOS Inverter

## Topology

This is the classic **CMOS inverter (logic NOT gate)** — the most fundamental building block in digital CMOS. The two transistors are stacked in series between $V_{DD}$ and ground:

| Transistor | Type | Source | Gate | Drain |
|-----------|------|--------|------|-------|
| **M₁** (top) | PMOS (pull‑up) | $V_{DD}$ | $V_{in}$ | $V_{out}$ |
| **M₂** (bottom) | NMOS (pull‑down) | GND | $V_{in}$ | $V_{out}$ |

Both **gates** tie together to the input $V_{in}$; both **drains** tie together to the output $V_{out}$.

## DC Operation (the two static states)

The transistors work **complementarily** — one is on while the other is off.

**Case 1 — $V_{in}$ = HIGH (≈ $V_{DD}$):**
- M₂ (NMOS): $V_{GS2}=V_{DD}>V_{Tn}$ → **ON**
- M₁ (PMOS): $V_{SG1}=V_{DD}-V_{in}\approx 0 < |V_{Tp}|$ → **OFF**
- Output pulled to ground: $\boxed{V_{out}=0}$

**Case 2 — $V_{in}$ = LOW (≈ 0):**
- M₂ (NMOS): $V_{GS2}=0<V_{Tn}$ → **OFF**
- M₁ (PMOS): $V_{SG1}=V_{DD}>|V_{Tp}|$ → **ON**
- Output pulled to supply: $\boxed{V_{out}=V_{DD}}$

$$\therefore\quad V_{out}=\overline{V_{in}}\qquad\text{(logic inversion)}$$

## Voltage Transfer Characteristic (regions)

As $V_{in}$ sweeps $0 \to V_{DD}$, the circuit passes through five regions:

| Region | $V_{in}$ | M₁ (PMOS) | M₂ (NMOS) | $V_{out}$ |
|--------|----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| 1 | $< V_{Tn}$ | triode | off | $V_{DD}$ |
| 2 | low | triode | **sat** | falling |
| 3 | $\approx V_M$ | **sat** | **sat** | steep drop (high gain) |
| 4 | high | **sat** | triode | near 0 |
| 5 | $>V_{DD}-\lvert V_{Tp}\rvert$ | off | triode | 0 |

The transition is sharp because in Region 3 both devices are saturated → very high small‑signal gain.

## Switching Threshold

Setting both saturation currents equal at $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$:

$$V_M=\frac{(V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|)+\sqrt{k_n/k_p}\;V_{Tn}}{1+\sqrt{k_n/k_p}},\qquad k=\mu C_{ox}\tfrac{W}{L}$$

If the devices are matched ($k_n=k_p$, $V_{Tn}=|V_{Tp}|$), then $V_M=V_{DD}/2$. (Since $\mu_n>\mu_p$, the PMOS is usually made wider to balance this.)

## Key Properties

- ⚡ **Zero static power:** In both steady states one transistor is off → no DC path from $V_{DD}$ to GND (only leakage). Power is consumed only *during* switching.
- 📈 **Rail-to-rail output:** full swing $0 \leftrightarrow V_{DD}$, giving excellent noise margins.
- 🔌 **Infinite DC input resistance:** gates are capacitive; no steady gate current.
- 🔥 **Short-circuit current spike:** near $V_{in}=V_M$ both transistors conduct briefly, drawing a transient current pulse from the supply.

**In short:** this is a CMOS inverter that outputs the logical complement of its input, with full-swing output and essentially no static power dissipation.

*(Identification check: the series stack with a shared gate node and shared drain node between $V_{DD}$ and ground only functions correctly if M₁ is the PMOS pull-up and M₂ the NMOS pull-down — two devices of the same type here would not form a usable logic gate.)*

## Identifying the circuit

Both **M1 and M2 are n‑channel MOSFETs (NMOS)** — their source arrows have the same orientation (a CMOS inverter would show the two arrows pointing in *opposite* directions, with a PMOS on top). They are stacked between $V_{DD}$ and ground, gates tied together to $V_{in}$, output taken from the middle node:

| Device | Connections | Role |
|--------|-------------|------|
| **M1** (top) | drain → $V_{DD}$, source → $V_{out}$ | common‑drain (**source follower**), pull‑up |
| **M2** (bottom) | drain → $V_{out}$, source → GND | **common‑source**, pull‑down |

So it has the "totem‑pole" look of an inverter, **but it is not a CMOS inverter** because the top device is an NMOS, not a PMOS.

## Large‑signal behavior (sweep $V_{in}$ from 0 → $V_{DD}$)

**$V_{in} < V_{th}$:** $V_{GS2}=V_{in}<V_{th}$ → M2 off. M1 would need $V_{out} < V_{in}-V_{th} < 0$ to conduct → M1 off too. **Both off → the output floats (high‑impedance).**

**$V_{in} > V_{th}$:** both conduct, so a **DC current flows continuously** from $V_{DD}$ through M1 and M2 (static power). The follower M1 pulls up, the common‑source M2 pulls down, and they settle where $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$.

Because $V_{DD}$ is high, M1 stays in **saturation**; because the follower keeps $V_{out}$ below $V_{in}-V_{th}$, M2 is in the **triode** region:

$$I_{D1}=\tfrac12 k_1\,(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{th})^2,\qquad I_{D2}=k_2\big[(V_{in}-V_{th})V_{out}-\tfrac12 V_{out}^2\big]$$

Setting them equal gives the transfer characteristic:

$$\boxed{\,V_{out}=(V_{in}-V_{th})\left[\,1-\sqrt{\dfrac{k_2}{k_1+k_2}}\,\right]\,},\qquad k=\mu_n C_{ox}\tfrac{W}{L}$$

## Key observations

- **Non‑inverting:** $V_{out}$ *rises* with $V_{in}$ — the opposite of an inverter.
- **Gain < 1:** slope $=1-\sqrt{k_2/(k_1+k_2)}\in(0,1)$. For matched devices ($k_1=k_2$) this is $\approx 0.29$.
- **Poor swing:** output only spans roughly $0$ to $0.29\,(V_{DD}-V_{th})$ for matched devices — far from rail‑to‑rail — and it *floats* when $V_{in}$ is low.
- **Static power** whenever both transistors are on.
- **Body effect** on M1 (its source sits at $V_{out}$, not ground) raises $V_{th1}$ and weakens the pull‑up even further.

## Small‑signal view

Doing KCL at the output node gives

$$A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=1-\sqrt{\frac{k_2}{k_1+k_2}}\approx 0.29\ \text{(matched)}$$

i.e. a **non‑inverting, less‑than‑unity stage** — essentially a lossy source follower whose bias current (set by M2) is modulated by the same input.

## Bottom line

This is a **source follower (M1) with a common‑source pull‑down (M2) driven by the same input**. It makes a **poor inverter** (non‑inverting, limited swing, floating low state, static current) and a **poor amplifier** (gain < 1).

To get a *proper* inverter, replace the top NMOS with a **PMOS whose source goes to $V_{DD}$** → the standard **CMOS inverter**: rail‑to‑rail output, essentially no static current, and high gain at the switching point.

*(If your figure actually shows the top device as a PMOS, let me know and I'll give the CMOS‑inverter analysis instead.)*

# Circuit Analysis

## What the circuit is

Two **N‑channel enhancement MOSFETs** are stacked in series between $V_{DD}$ and ground, with both gates tied to the common input $V_{in}$ and the output taken from the middle node:

| Device | Drain | Gate | Source | Configuration |
|--------|-------|------|--------|---------------|
| **M₁** (top) | $V_{DD}$ | $V_{in}$ | $V_{out}$ | Common‑drain (**source follower**) |
| **M₂** (bottom) | $V_{out}$ | $V_{in}$ | GND | Common‑source |

Both symbols are identical (source arrows point outward, source = lower terminal), so **both are NMOS**. This is therefore **not** a complementary (CMOS) inverter — there is no PMOS pull‑up.

## Qualitative operation

- **M₂ (pull‑down):** turns on when $V_{in} > V_{th}$ and pulls $V_{out}$ toward ground. ✔ A good pull‑down.
- **M₁ (pull‑up):** conducts only while $V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{out}>V_{th}$. As a source follower it can raise $V_{out}$ **only up to $V_{in}-V_{th}$**, where it shuts itself off. It can never reach $V_{DD}$, and it cannot pull the node down. ✘ A weak, lossy pull‑up.

## DC transfer characteristic

With no DC load, $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$. Taking M₁ in saturation and M₂ in triode:

$$\frac{k}{2}\,(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{th})^2 = k\!\left[(V_{in}-V_{th})V_{out}-\tfrac{V_{out}^2}{2}\right]$$

Letting $a = V_{in}-V_{th}$ gives $2V_{out}^2 - 4aV_{out}+a^2=0$, so for matched devices:

$$\boxed{V_{out}=\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2}\,(V_{in}-V_{th})\approx 0.29\,(V_{in}-V_{th})}$$

**Resulting behavior:**

| Input | Output |
|-------|--------|
| $V_{in}<V_{th}$ | Both devices **off → output floats** (high‑Z). Cannot be driven high. |
| $V_{in}>V_{th}$ | $V_{out}\approx 0.29(V_{in}-V_{th})$ — a small voltage that **rises** with $V_{in}$ |

## Key conclusion

This circuit **does not function as an inverter**:

- It is actually **non‑inverting** ($V_{out}$ *increases* with $V_{in}$) with **attenuation** (slope ≈ 0.29).
- It never produces a clean logic HIGH — the output maxes out near $0.29(V_{DD}-V_{th})$ and floats for low input.
- (Body effect on M₁, whose source sits at $V_{out}$, makes the pull‑up even weaker.)

**Root cause:** an NMOS is excellent at pulling a node *down* to ground but poor at pulling it *up* (a follower loses a threshold and turns off). A real inverter needs a **PMOS** in the M₁ position — i.e. the **CMOS inverter**, which gives full rail‑to‑rail, inverting operation. This circuit is essentially the "textbook counter‑example" that motivates CMOS.

> **Device‑type note:** If, in your figure, M₁ is actually drawn as a *PMOS* (bubble on gate, or source tied to $V_{DD}$), then this is the standard CMOS inverter and the behavior is the opposite — clean inverting, rail‑to‑rail, with essentially zero static current. The analysis above assumes the two symbols shown are identical NMOS devices.

# Circuit Analysis

## Topology Identification

| Device | Type | Role | Connections |
|--------|------|------|-------------|
| **M₁** | NMOS | Input / driver (common‑source) | Gate = $V_{in}$, Source = GND, Drain = $V_{out}$ |
| **M₂** | PMOS | **Diode‑connected** load | Source = $V_{DD}$, Gate = Drain = $V_{out}$ |

Since M₂'s gate is tied to its drain, it behaves as a two‑terminal "diode" element presenting a resistance of $\approx 1/g_{m2}$.

**→ This is a common‑source amplifier with a diode‑connected (active) load.**

## Operation

The two transistors are in series and carry the **same current**. M₁ converts the input voltage to a current, and M₂ converts that current back to a voltage drop below $V_{DD}$. Both devices operate in saturation (the diode‑connected M₂ is *always* in saturation while conducting, since $V_{SD2}=V_{SG2}$).

## Large‑Signal Transfer Characteristic

Equating drain currents:

$$\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_1 (V_{in}-V_{TN})^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_2 (V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{TP}|)^2$$

Solving for the output:

$$\boxed{V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|-\sqrt{\frac{\mu_n (W/L)_1}{\mu_p (W/L)_2}}\;(V_{in}-V_{TN})}$$

A key feature: **$V_{out}$ is a *linear* function of $V_{in}$** (as long as both stay saturated), which makes this a surprisingly linear amplifier.

## Small‑Signal Gain

$$A_v = -g_{m1}\left(r_{o1}\,\|\,r_{o2}\,\|\,\tfrac{1}{g_{m2}}\right)\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}$$

Substituting $g_m=\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$ with equal currents:

$$\boxed{A_v \approx -\sqrt{\frac{\mu_n (W/L)_1}{\mu_p (W/L)_2}}}$$

## Key Properties

- **Inverting** amplifier.
- **Gain set by geometry/mobility ratio**, *not* by bias current → very linear and well‑controlled, but **low** (only grows with the *square root* of the W/L ratio).
- **Output resistance:** $R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m2}$ (low).
- **Input resistance:** essentially infinite (MOS gate).

**Trade‑off:** Compared to a current‑source load (gain $\sim g_m r_o$), the diode load gives much lower gain but excellent linearity and wide bandwidth — it is the basic building block of the active‑load differential pair and simple gain stages.

# Circuit Analysis: Common-Source Amplifier with Diode-Connected Load

## Topology Identification

| Device | Type | Role | Connections |
|--------|------|------|-------------|
| **M₁** | NMOS | Input/driver transistor (common-source) | Gate = Vin, Source = GND, Drain = Vout |
| **M₂** | PMOS | **Diode-connected** active load | Source = V_DD, Gate = Drain = Vout |

Since M₂'s gate is tied to its drain, it behaves as a two-terminal "diode" load. This is a classic **common-source amplifier with a diode-connected PMOS load**.

## DC Operation

The two transistors are in series, so they carry the **same drain current**:

$$I_{D1} = I_{D2} = I_D$$

**M₁ (NMOS, saturation):**
$$I_D = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_1 (V_{in}-V_{TN})^2$$

**M₂ (PMOS, always saturated since $V_{DS}=V_{GS}$):**
$$I_D = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_2 (V_{SG2}-|V_{TP}|)^2,\qquad V_{out}=V_{DD}-V_{SG2}$$

## Small-Signal Gain

The resistance looking into the diode-connected M₂ is low:

$$R_{M2} = \frac{1}{g_{m2}}\,\Big\|\,r_{o2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

So the gain is:

$$\boxed{A_v = -g_{m1}\left(\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\,\Big\|\,r_{o1}\,\Big\|\,r_{o2}\right) \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}}$$

Substituting $g_m=\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$ (same $I_D$ cancels):

$$A_v \approx -\sqrt{\frac{\mu_n\,(W/L)_1}{\mu_p\,(W/L)_2}}$$

## Key Characteristics

✅ **Highly linear & predictable** — gain depends only on a *ratio* of geometries and mobilities, nearly **independent of bias current**, temperature, and process.

⚠️ **Low gain** — magnitude is only $\sqrt{(\mu_n/\mu_p)(W/L)_1/(W/L)_2}$, typically just **2–5×**. Achieving even 10× requires a (W/L)₁/(W/L)₂ ratio of ~30–50.

⚠️ **Reduced output swing** — the load needs $V_{SG2}\ge|V_{TP}|$, so the output cannot rise above:
$$V_{out,max} = V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$$

✅ **Low output impedance** (≈ 1/g_{m2}) → good drive capability and wide bandwidth.

## Summary
This stage trades gain for **excellent linearity and a well-defined gain set by device sizing** — commonly used in broadband amplifiers, output buffers, and gain stages where a precise, low, bias-insensitive gain is desired (a resistive-type load without using actual resistors).

# Circuit Analysis

## Topology Identification

Looking at the devices:

| Device | Type | Role | Connections |
|--------|------|------|-------------|
| **M₁** | NMOS (arrow out of source) | Driver / input transistor | Gate = Vᵢₙ, Source = GND, Drain = Vₒᵤₜ |
| **M₂** | PMOS (arrow into source) | Active load | Source = V_DD, **Gate tied to Drain** (diode-connected), Drain = Vₒᵤₜ |

Since **only M₁'s gate** receives the input while **M₂'s gate is shorted to its drain**, this is a:

> **Common-Source amplifier (M₁) with a diode-connected PMOS active load (M₂)**

(Note: this is *not* a CMOS inverter — that would require both gates driven by Vᵢₙ.)

## DC / Bias Analysis

Both transistors carry the same drain current $I_D$:

$$I_{D1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_1 (V_{in}-V_{Tn})^2$$

$$I_{D2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_2 (V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{Tp}|)^2$$

M₂ is **always in saturation** (because $V_{DS}=V_{GS}$ for a diode connection). M₁ stays in saturation as long as:

$$V_{out} \ge V_{in}-V_{Tn}$$

## Small-Signal Gain

A diode-connected transistor behaves like a resistor of value $\approx 1/g_{m2}$. The output node therefore sees:

$$R_{out} = \frac{1}{g_{m2}} \;\big\|\; r_{o2} \;\big\|\; r_{o1} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

The voltage gain is:

$$\boxed{A_v = -g_{m1}\left(\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\,\|\,r_{o1}\,\|\,r_{o2}\right) \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}}$$

Since both devices share the same current $I_D$, using $g_m=\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$:

$$A_v \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} = -\sqrt{\frac{\mu_n (W/L)_1}{\mu_p (W/L)_2}}$$

- **Input resistance:** $R_{in} = \infty$ (MOS gate)
- **Output resistance:** $R_{out} \approx 1/g_{m2}$

## Key Takeaways

✅ **Advantages**
- Gain is set almost entirely by a **ratio of device geometries** $(W/L)_1/(W/L)_2$ and mobilities — very **insensitive to temperature, supply, and bias current** variations, giving good linearity.

⚠️ **Limitations**
- **Low gain** — the gain is only $\sqrt{(\mu_n/\mu_p)(W/L)_1/(W/L)_2}$, which is hard to make large (increasing the ratio requires huge $W/L$ differences).
- **Reduced output swing** — the diode-connected load always drops at least $|V_{Tp}|$, limiting the maximum $V_{out}$.

# Circuit Analysis

## Topology Identification

Both transistors are **N-channel MOSFETs** (the source arrows point *inward*, toward the gate/channel).

**Transistor M₂ (top):**
- Drain → V_DD
- Gate → V_in (input)
- Source → V_out (output)

→ This is a **common‑drain (source‑follower)** configuration.

**Transistor M₁ (bottom):**
- Drain → V_out
- Gate → ground
- Source → ground  (so V_GS1 = 0)

→ With gate and source tied together at ground, M₁ conducts a fixed current only if it is a **depletion‑mode device**. It therefore behaves as a **current‑source / active load** (I_D1 ≈ I_DSS, with large output resistance r_o1).

**Conclusion: This is an NMOS source follower (M₂) biased by a current‑source load (M₁) — i.e., a unity‑gain voltage buffer.**

## DC Operation

M₂ carries the bias current set by M₁. Since V_GS2 is approximately constant,

$$V_{out} = V_{in} - V_{GS2}$$

The output **tracks the input** (non-inverting) with a fixed DC level shift of V_GS2.

## Small-Signal Analysis

Let $R = r_{o1}\,\|\,r_{o2}$ (load = current-source output resistance in parallel with M₂'s own r_o).

**Voltage gain:**
$$A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{g_{m2}\,R}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,R} \;\approx\; \frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \lesssim 1$$

- Without body effect → $A_v \approx 1$
- With body effect ($g_{mb}=\chi g_m$, $\chi\approx0.1$–0.2) → $A_v \approx 0.8$–0.9

**Input resistance** (looking into the gate):
$$R_{in} \rightarrow \infty \quad(\text{very high})$$

**Output resistance** (looking into M₂'s source):
$$R_{out} = \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\,\Big\|\,r_{o1}\,\Big\|\,r_{o2} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \quad(\text{low})$$

## Summary of Function

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Configuration | Source follower (common-drain) |
| Voltage gain | ≈ +1 (slightly less) |
| Phase | Non-inverting |
| Input impedance | Very high |
| Output impedance | Low (≈ 1/g_m) |
| DC shift | V_out = V_in − V_GS2 |

**Purpose:** A **voltage buffer / impedance converter** — it presents a high impedance to the driving stage and a low impedance to the load, allowing it to drive heavy (low-impedance) loads without attenuation. It also serves as a **DC level shifter**.

> *Note:* For M₁ to supply bias current with V_GS = 0 it must be a depletion-mode device (or treated as an ideal current source). If M₁ were an enhancement device, it would be cut off and the circuit would not bias correctly.

# Circuit Analysis

## Device identification

Both transistors are **PMOS**. The clue is the arrow on the source lead: it points **inward (toward the gate)**, which is the p‑channel convention. (An NMOS source arrow points outward.) Consistently, the source — the terminal carrying the arrow — sits on the *higher‑potential* side of each device.

| Transistor | Source | Gate | Drain |
|-----------|--------|------|-------|
| **M₂** (top) | V_DD | V_in | V_out |
| **M₁** (bottom) | V_out | GND | GND |

Because M₁'s **gate and drain are both grounded**, M₁ is **diode‑connected** (V_GD = 0).

## Configuration

- **M₂ → common‑source stage:** its source is at V_DD (AC ground), the signal enters the gate, and the output is taken at the drain.
- **M₁ → diode‑connected active load:** it behaves as a two‑terminal nonlinear "resistor" of small‑signal value ≈ 1/g_m1 between V_out and ground.

➡️ **This is a common‑source amplifier with a diode‑connected (active) load — an inverting voltage amplifier.**

## DC operation

The two devices are in series, so I_D1 = I_D2:

$$I_{D2}=\tfrac12\mu_pC_{ox}\Big(\tfrac{W}{L}\Big)_2\!\big(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|\big)^2$$
$$I_{D1}=\tfrac12\mu_pC_{ox}\Big(\tfrac{W}{L}\Big)_1\!\big(V_{out}-|V_{tp}|\big)^2$$

Equating them:

$$\boxed{V_{out}=|V_{tp}|+\sqrt{\tfrac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}\;\big(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|\big)}$$

So while both devices stay in saturation, **V_out is a linear function of V_in**.

## Small‑signal gain

$$A_v=\frac{dV_{out}}{dV_{in}}=-\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}\approx-\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}$$

- **Inverting** (V_in ↑ ⇒ V_SG2 ↓ ⇒ less current ⇒ V_out ↓).
- Gain depends only on the **W/L ratio** — essentially independent of bias current and process, giving a very predictable, linear amplifier.
- The trade‑off is modest gain (e.g., a 100:1 size ratio yields only |A_v| = 10). *(A small body‑effect term g_mb1 appears if M₁'s body is tied to V_DD rather than its source.)*

## Impedances

- **Input:** ≈ ∞ (gate of M₂).
- **Output:** ≈ 1/g_m1 (set by the diode‑connected load) — low.

## Summary

A **PMOS common‑source amplifier (M₂) with a diode‑connected PMOS load (M₁)**: an inverting stage with high input impedance, low (~1/g_m1) output impedance, and a well‑controlled gain of about $-\sqrt{(W/L)_2/(W/L)_1}$.

Both transistors are drawn as **3‑terminal MOSFETs** with the source‑arrow pointing *inward* (toward the gate), and in each case that arrow sits on the terminal tied to the **higher** potential:

| Device | Source | Gate | Drain | Type |
|--------|--------|------|-------|------|
| **M₂** | V_DD | V_in | V_out | PMOS |
| **M₁** | V_out | GND | GND | PMOS |

An inward source arrow (current entering the source) = **PMOS**. For M₂ the source must sit at V_DD, and for M₁ the source must sit at V_out — the only labeling consistent with PMOS operation.

**Configuration:** This is a **common‑source amplifier with a diode‑connected load**.
- **M₂** = the gain (driver) transistor — input at its gate, source held at the AC‑ground V_DD → *common source*.
- **M₁** = the load — its gate and drain are both tied to ground (gate = drain) → *diode‑connected*, acting as a two‑terminal resistive element at the output.

The DC current path is: **V_DD → M₂ → V_out → M₁ → GND**.

## Large‑Signal (DC) Behavior

With both devices in saturation:

$$I_{D2}=\tfrac12 k_p\!\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_2\!\big(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|\big)^2 
\quad=\quad 
I_{D1}=\tfrac12 k_p\!\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_1\!\big(V_{out}-|V_{tp}|\big)^2$$

Equating the currents and solving:

$$\boxed{V_{out}=|V_{tp}|+\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}\;\big(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|\big)}$$

So **V_out is a nearly linear function of V_in** with a negative slope → the stage **inverts**.

## Small‑Signal Gain

The diode‑connected load M₁ presents a resistance of $1/g_{m1}$ (‖ r_{o1}) looking into its source. The gain is:

$$A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-g_{m2}\left(\frac{1}{g_{m1}}\;\Big\|\;r_{o1}\;\Big\|\;r_{o2}\right)\approx-\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}$$

Since both devices carry the **same current** and share $k_p$:

$$\boxed{A_v \approx -\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}=-\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}}$$

## Key Takeaways

- **Inverting amplifier** with a **gain set purely by the device‑size ratio** — essentially independent of bias current and process parameters.
- **Very linear** transfer characteristic (the √ of a ratio appears, not a squared term).
- **Moderate/low gain** — to get large gain you'd need an impractically large W/L ratio, which is why true gain stages usually replace the diode load with a current‑source load.
- **Low output resistance** $R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m1}$, and essentially **infinite input resistance** (MOS gate).

*(Gain assumes both transistors in saturation; including channel‑length modulation and M₁'s body effect gives $A_v=-g_{m2}/(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})$ in parallel with the r_o's.)*

## Circuit Analysis

This is a **cascode current source** (PMOS). The output resistance is seen looking into the **drain of M₁**, which has resistance $r_{O2}$ at its source (node X), provided by M₂.

## Using the Source-Degeneration Formula

For a transistor with a resistance $R_S$ at its source, the resistance looking into the drain is:

$$R_{out} = \left[1 + (g_m + g_{mb})r_O\right]R_S + r_O$$

## Applying to M₁

Here, the degeneration resistance at the source of M₁ is $R_S = r_{O2}$:

$$\boxed{R_{out} = \left[1 + (g_{m1} + g_{mb1})r_{O1}\right]r_{O2} + r_{O1}}$$

Expanding:

$$R_{out} = r_{O1} + r_{O2} + (g_{m1} + g_{mb1})\,r_{O1}\,r_{O2}$$

## Simplified Result

Since $(g_{m1} + g_{mb1})\,r_{O1} \gg 1$, this reduces to:

$$R_{out} \approx (g_{m1} + g_{mb1})\,r_{O1}\,r_{O2}$$

**Key insight:** The cascode device M₁ *boosts* the output resistance of M₂ (which alone would be $r_{O2}$) by a factor of approximately $g_{m1}r_{O1}$.

## Setting Up the Problem

In this figure, **M₂ is a PMOS device** with its **source at V_DD** and its **drain at node X**. (M₁ is the cascode transistor below it, and the output resistance R_out is seen looking into M₁'s drain.)

## Saturation Condition for M₂

A PMOS transistor is in saturation when

$$|V_{DS}| \geq |V_{GS}| - |V_{THP}| \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V_{SD2} \geq V_{OV2}$$

For M₂:

$$V_{SD2} = V_{DD} - V_X \qquad V_{OV2} = V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}| = (V_{DD}-V_{b2}) - |V_{THP}|$$

Substituting:

$$V_{DD} - V_X \;\geq\; (V_{DD}-V_{b2}) - |V_{THP}|$$

$$\boxed{V_X \leq V_{b2} + |V_{THP}|}$$

**In words:** the voltage at node X must stay *below* $V_{b2}+|V_{THP}|$ — equivalently, V_X must sit at least one overdrive ($V_{OV2}$) *below* V_DD.

## How Biasing Ensures It

Node X is set by M₁. To carry the bias current, M₁ needs $V_{SG1} = |V_{THP}| + V_{OV1}$, so:

$$V_X = V_{b1} + |V_{THP}| + V_{OV1}$$

Plugging this into the saturation condition:

$$V_{b1} + |V_{THP}| + V_{OV1} \;\leq\; V_{b2} + |V_{THP}|$$

$$\boxed{V_{b2} \geq V_{b1} + V_{OV1}}$$

## Takeaway

We keep M₂ in saturation by **choosing the gate bias voltages properly** — specifically, making $V_{b2}$ exceed $V_{b1}$ by at least the overdrive of M₁. This holds node X low enough ($V_X \le V_{DD} - V_{OV2}$) so that M₂ retains sufficient source–drain voltage. In practice $V_{b2}$ is generated to place X just below $V_{DD}-V_{OV2}$, which keeps M₂ in saturation while preserving maximum output voltage swing.

# Cascode Amplifier Analysis

## Circuit Identification

This is a **cascode amplifier with an active (current‑source) load**:

| Device | Role | Configuration |
|--------|------|---------------|
| $M_1$ | Input transistor | Common‑source (signal on gate, source grounded) |
| $M_2$ | Cascode transistor | Common‑gate (gate at fixed bias $V_{b1}$ = AC ground) |
| $I_1$ | Load | Ideal current source from $V_{DD}$ |

**Signal flow:** $v_{in}$ drives $M_1$, which converts the input voltage to a drain current. This current passes (with ~unity current gain) up through the common‑gate device $M_2$ and develops the output voltage across the high output resistance at $v_{out}$.

## DC / Bias Analysis

Since the devices are stacked in series with the current source:
$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1$$

Node voltages:
$$V_X = V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$$

**Saturation conditions:**
- $M_1$: $\;V_X \ge V_{ov1}\;\Rightarrow\; V_{b1}\ge V_{GS2}+V_{ov1}$
- $M_2$: $\;V_{out}-V_X \ge V_{ov2}$

**Minimum output voltage** (both devices saturated):
$$V_{out,\min}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$$

## Small-Signal Analysis

**Output resistance** (looking into $M_2$'s drain, with $M_1$ presenting $r_{o1}$ at the source of $M_2$):
$$R_{out}= r_{o2}+r_{o1}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}r_{o1}\;\approx\;(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

This is the key effect: $M_2$ **boosts** $r_{o1}$ by its own intrinsic gain. With an ideal $I_1$ this is the full output resistance; with a real source, place it in parallel with $R_{I1}$.

**Overall transconductance:** all of $M_1$'s signal current reaches the output, so
$$G_m \approx g_{m1}$$

**Voltage gain:**
$$\boxed{A_v = -G_m R_{out}\;\approx\; -g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o1}r_{o2}}$$

(Neglecting body effect: $A_v\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}\,r_{o1}r_{o2}$.) This is roughly the **square** of a single CS stage's gain $(g_m r_o)^2$.

**Input resistance:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (MOS gate, low frequency).

**Gain at node X:**
$$\frac{v_X}{v_{in}}\approx-\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\approx-1$$

## Why Cascode? (Advantages)

- ✅ **Very high gain / output resistance** — ideal for high-gain stages and current mirrors.
- ✅ **Reduced Miller effect** → better bandwidth. Because node X sees only ~$-1$ gain, $C_{GD1}$ is barely multiplied, keeping the input capacitance small.
- ✅ **Good input–output isolation** (reverse isolation).

## Trade-offs (Drawbacks)

- ❌ **Reduced output swing** — headroom consumed is $V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$.
- ❌ Requires an extra bias voltage $V_{b1}$.

# Circuit Identification

This is a **cascode amplifier** (a telescopic cascode stage) with an ideal current-source load:

| Device | Role | Configuration |
|--------|------|---------------|
| $M_1$ | Input transistor | Common-source (gate = $v_{in}$) |
| $M_2$ | Cascode transistor | Common-gate (gate = $V_{b1}$, a fixed bias) |
| $I_1$ | Active load | Ideal current source (sets bias current) |

The output is taken at the drain of $M_2$.

# Operation / Signal Path

- $M_1$ converts the input voltage into a signal current: $i_d \approx g_{m1}\,v_{in}$.
- $M_2$ (gate held at AC ground by $V_{b1}$) routes this current to the output node while **shielding** node $X$ from the large output swing.
- $I_1$ acts as a high-impedance load, so the signal current develops a large voltage across the output resistance.

# DC Bias & Headroom

The bias current $I_1$ flows through both transistors. For both to stay in **saturation**:

$$V_X \ge V_{OV1}, \qquad V_{out}-V_X \ge V_{OV2}$$

Since $V_X = V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$, the minimum output level is:

$$\boxed{V_{out,\min} = V_{OV1} + V_{OV2}}$$

To maximize output swing, choose $V_{b1} = V_{GS2} + V_{OV1}$ (keeps $M_1$ just at the edge of saturation).

# Small-Signal Analysis

**Transconductance** (output shorted):

$$G_m = \frac{g_{m1}\,(g_{m2}+1/r_{O2})}{g_{m2}+1/r_{O2}+1/r_{O1}} \;\approx\; g_{m1}$$

**Output resistance** (looking into drain of $M_2$, with $r_{O1}$ as source degeneration; $I_1$ ideal ⇒ infinite):

$$R_{out} = r_{O2} + r_{O1} + g_{m2}r_{O2}r_{O1} \;\approx\; g_{m2}r_{O2}r_{O1}$$

**Voltage gain:**

$$A_v = -G_m R_{out} = -g_{m1}r_{O1}\,(1+g_{m2}r_{O2})$$

$$\boxed{A_v \approx -\,g_{m1}g_{m2}\,r_{O1}r_{O2} \;=\; -(g_m r_o)^2\text{-type gain}}$$

| Node $X$ | Low-impedance intermediate node (source of $M_2$ / drain of $M_1$) |

The current source $I_1$ forces the DC bias current through the series stack $M_2$–$M_1$:

$$I_{D1} = I_{D2} = I_1$$

- $v_{in}$ (DC level) sets $M_1$'s operating point.
- $V_{b1}$ holds $M_2$'s gate at a fixed voltage, pinning node $X$ at roughly $V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$.

# Small-Signal Analysis

**Transconductance of the stage** — $M_1$ converts input voltage to current, which $M_2$ passes straight through:

$$G_m = g_{m1}$$

**Output resistance** — looking into the drain of $M_2$, $M_1$ acts as a source-degeneration resistance $r_{o1}$. $M_2$ "boosts" this:

$$R_{out} = r_{o2} + r_{o1} + (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o2}\,r_{o1} \;\approx\; (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o2}\,r_{o1}$$

(With an *ideal* current source, $I_1$ contributes infinite impedance, so the full $R_{out}$ is preserved.)

**Voltage gain:**

$$\boxed{A_v = -G_m R_{out} \approx -g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o2}\,r_{o1}}$$

Neglecting body effect, for matched devices this is on the order of $-(g_m r_o)^2$ — much larger than a simple CS stage's $-g_m r_o$.

# Output Swing (Headroom)

Both transistors must stay in saturation. The minimum output voltage is:

$$V_{out,\min} = V_{OV1} + V_{OV2}$$

This loss of voltage headroom is the main cost of cascoding.

# Why Use This Topology

✅ **High output resistance** → **high voltage gain**

✅ **Reduced Miller effect**: node $X$ has low gain ($\approx g_{m1}/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\sim 1$), so $M_1$'s $C_{GD}$ is barely multiplied → **wider bandwidth**

✅ **Good input–output isolation** (shielding by $M_2$ reduces reverse feedback)

❌ **Reduced output swing** (extra $V_{OV}$ dropped across $M_2$)

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
## The Miller Effect, Briefly

When a capacitance $C_f$ bridges the input and output of an inverting amplifier with voltage gain $A_v$, it appears at the input *amplified*:

$$C_{\text{Miller}} = C_f\,(1 + |A_v|)$$

In a common-source (CS) or common-emitter (CE) stage, the gate–drain capacitance $C_{gd}$ (or base–collector $C_\mu$) is exactly such a bridging capacitance. Since the stage gain $A_v = -g_m R_L$ is large, the input sees a big effective capacitance. Combined with the source resistance, this forms the **dominant input pole** that kills bandwidth:

$$f_p \approx \frac{1}{2\pi R_s C_{\text{Miller}}}$$

So the problem is: **high gain and the bridging capacitance both act at the same node.**

## What the Cascode Does

A cascode stacks a common-gate/common-base (CG/CB) transistor on top of the CS/CE input transistor:

- Input transistor $M_1$ (CS): signal enters its gate
- Cascode transistor $M_2$ (CG): gate held at fixed DC (AC ground), output taken at its drain

The trick is **where the gain is developed.**

The CG transistor $M_2$ presents a *low* input resistance looking into its source:

$$R_{\text{in},2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

This low resistance is the load that $M_1$ actually drives. So the voltage gain *across $M_1$* — the gain that matters for its Miller capacitance — is only:

$$A_{v1} = -g_{m1}\cdot R_{\text{in},2} \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1$$

(for matched devices). Therefore the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ collapses:

$$C_{\text{Miller}} = C_{gd1}(1 + |A_{v1}|) \approx 2\,C_{gd1}$$

instead of $C_{gd1}(1 + g_m R_L)$, which could be tens to hundreds of times larger.

## Where Did the Gain Go?

The overall gain hasn't been lost — it's just been **relocated**. The full large gain ($\approx -g_{m1} R_L$) now develops at the *output node* (drain of $M_2$), where the CG transistor delivers the current into the high output impedance. Crucially, that large gain no longer appears across $M_1$'s bridging capacitance.

Meanwhile, $M_2$ itself doesn't suffer Miller multiplication: its gate is grounded, so its $C_{gd2}$ simply ties the output node to AC ground rather than feeding gain back to a sensitive input.

## Summary

| | Plain CS/CE | Cascode |
|---|---|---|
| Gain across input device's $C_{gd}/C_\mu$ | $-g_m R_L$ (large) | $\approx -1$ |
| Miller capacitance | $C_f(1+g_m R_L)$ | $\approx 2C_f$ |
| Input pole / bandwidth | low | much higher |

The essential reason: **the cascode transistor "shields" the input device by holding its drain/collector at a low, nearly constant impedance**, so the input transistor operates with unity gain across its feedback capacitance. The high gain is restored downstream, isolated from the input. This decoupling of gain from the Miller node is why cascodes achieve high gain *and* wide bandwidth simultaneously.

The main explanation and conclusion match the golden solution.

answer.text:
## The Miller Effect, Briefly

In a common-source (or common-emitter) stage, the feedback capacitance between input and output—$C_{gd}$ for a MOSFET, $C_\mu$ for a BJT—gets amplified by the stage's voltage gain. A capacitance $C_f$ bridging the input and output of an inverting amplifier with gain $-A$ appears at the input as:

$$C_{in} = C_f\,(1 + A)$$

The reason is simple charge accounting: if the input moves by $\Delta V$, the output swings by $-A\,\Delta V$, so the voltage *across* $C_f$ changes by $(1+A)\,\Delta V$. The input node must supply $(1+A)$ times as much charge, so the capacitor "looks" $(1+A)$ times bigger.

This bloated input capacitance combines with the source resistance to form a low-frequency pole, $f_p \approx 1/(2\pi R_s C_{in})$, which kills the bandwidth.

## The Cascode Trick

A cascode stacks a **common-gate** device (M2) on top of the **common-source** input device (M1), with M2's gate held at AC ground:

- M1: input transistor, common-source
- M2: cascode transistor, common-gate, gate at fixed bias
- Drain of M1 → source of M2

The key fact is the **input impedance looking into the source of M2**, which is low:

$$R_{in,M2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

So M1 no longer drives a large load resistance ($r_o$) at its drain—it drives this small $1/g_{m2}$ instead. The gain *of the input stage* collapses to:

$$A_{v1} = -g_{m1}\cdot\frac{1}{g_{m2}} = -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1$$

(for matched devices). Now the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is only:

$$C_{in} = C_{gd1}\left(1 + \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\right) \approx 2\,C_{gd1}$$

Compare that to a plain common-source stage, where the factor is $(1 + g_m r_o)$—easily hundreds or thousands. The input pole moves up by roughly the same factor.

## Where Did the Gain Go? (It Didn't Disappear)

You still get the full gain—it's just relocated to a node that doesn't have a Miller problem. The current from M1 passes through M2 into the high output resistance, so:

$$A_{v,\text{total}} \approx -g_{m1}\,R_{out}$$

The cascode stage (common-gate) is immune to the Miller effect because **its grounded gate sits between the input (source) and output (drain), acting as an electrostatic shield.** There is no capacitance directly bridging source and drain:
- $C_{gs2}$ connects the input node to AC ground
- $C_{gd2}$ connects the output node to AC ground

Neither is a feedback path, so neither gets multiplied.

## The Bottom Line

The cascode **splits the amplifier into a low-gain front end and a high-gain back end.**

| | Common-source | Cascode input stage (M1) |
|---|---|---|
| Load at drain | $r_o$ (large) | $1/g_{m2}$ (small) |
| Stage gain | $-g_m r_o$ | $\approx -1$ |
| Miller cap | $C_{gd}(1+g_m r_o)$ | $\approx 2C_{gd}$ |

By denying $C_{gd1}$ any voltage gain to multiply against, and by producing the remaining gain in a topology with no feedback capacitance, the cascode pushes the input pole to much higher frequencies—giving you high gain **and** wide bandwidth at the same time.

answer.text:
## The Miller Effect in Brief

Any inverting voltage amplifier has a small capacitance bridging its input and output:
- **BJT common-emitter:** the base–collector capacitance $C_\mu$
- **MOSFET common-source:** the gate–drain capacitance $C_{gd}$

Because this capacitor spans a node that swings in the *opposite* direction (and by a large factor) from the input, it appears at the input amplified by the Miller factor:

$$C_{\text{in,Miller}} = C_f\,(1 - A_v)$$

where $A_v = v_{out}/v_{in}$ is negative. For an inverting stage with gain magnitude $|A_v|$, this becomes $C_f(1+|A_v|)$. This inflated input capacitance forms an RC low-pass filter with the source resistance and **sets the dominant high-frequency pole**, limiting bandwidth.

## Why a Single CE/CS Stage Is Bad

In a plain common-emitter stage, the voltage gain is large:

$$A_v \approx -g_m R_L \quad (\text{e.g., } -100)$$

So $C_\mu$ is multiplied by roughly 100 — a large input capacitance and a low bandwidth.

## What the Cascode Changes

A cascode stacks a **common-base (common-gate)** transistor Q2 on top of the **common-emitter (common-source)** input transistor Q1:

- Q1's collector/drain no longer drives the big load resistor $R_L$.
- Instead it drives the **emitter/source of Q2**, which presents a *low* input impedance of about $1/g_{m2}$.

The key consequence is that the **voltage gain across Q1 collapses**:

$$A_{v1} \approx -g_{m1}\cdot\frac{1}{g_{m2}} = -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1$$

(≈ −1 when Q1 and Q2 share the same bias current). The Miller multiplication of Q1's feedback capacitance is therefore only:

$$C_{\text{in,Miller}} = C_\mu\,(1 - (-1)) = 2\,C_\mu$$

Instead of ×100, it's just ×2. The dominant input pole is pushed to a much higher frequency.

## But the Gain Isn't Lost

The overall gain is preserved — it's just delivered somewhere harmless:

- Q1 still converts input voltage to current: $i = g_{m1}v_{in}$
- Q2 passes that current to the output almost unchanged ($\alpha \approx 1$)
- The output node sees the full load: $v_{out} \approx -g_{m1}R_L\,v_{in}$

So the gain magnitude is still $g_{m1}R_L$, but it develops at **Q2's collector/drain**, not across Q1.

## Why Q2 Doesn't Reintroduce the Problem

In the common-base/common-gate stage, the base/gate is at AC ground. Q2's $C_\mu$ (or $C_{gd}$) therefore connects the output node to ground rather than bridging output back to input — **there is no feedback path to Miller-multiply**. The common-base stage is inherently a wideband configuration.

## Summary

| | Gain across input device | Miller multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| Common-emitter alone | $-g_m R_L$ (large) | $\sim(1+g_m R_L)$ |
| Cascode (Q1) | $-g_{m1}/g_{m2}\approx -1$ | $\sim 2$ |

The cascode works by **presenting a low-impedance load to the input transistor**, forcing its local voltage gain toward unity. This starves the Miller effect while the common-base stage recovers the full gain at a node that has no input–output feedback capacitance — giving you high gain *and* high bandwidth.

# Circuit Analysis

## Topology Identification

This is a **common‑gate (CG) amplifier with a PMOS current‑source (active) load.**

| Device | Type | Terminals | Role |
|--------|------|-----------|------|
| **M₁** | PMOS | Source → V_DD, Gate → V_b2 (DC), Drain → V_out | Current‑source load |
| **M₂** | NMOS | Source → V_in, Gate → V_b1 (DC), Drain → V_out | Common‑gate input device |

**Why common‑gate?** The input signal is applied to the **source** of M₂ (note the arrow terminal where V_in enters), the gate is held at a fixed DC bias V_b1 (an AC ground), and the output is taken at the **drain**. Input‑at‑source / output‑at‑drain / gate‑grounded = common gate.

**Why M₁ is a current source:** Its gate (V_b2) and source (V_DD) are both at fixed potentials, so V_SG is constant. It therefore delivers a nearly constant current and presents a large small‑signal resistance **r_o1** at the output node.

## DC Operation
- V_b2 sets the bias current through M₁.
- V_b1 and the DC level of V_in set M₂'s operating point.
- Both transistors must remain in **saturation** for linear gain.

## Small‑Signal Analysis
Let $G_{m2} = g_{m2} + g_{mb2}$ (body effect is present because the source of M₂ moves with V_in).

**Voltage gain (non‑inverting):**
$$A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{1 + G_{m2}r_{o2}}{1+\frac{r_{o2}}{r_{o1}}} \cdot\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}\;\approx\; +\,G_{m2}\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

*Intuition:* V_in↑ ⟹ V_GS2 = V_b1 − V_in ↓ ⟹ M₂ sinks less current ⟹ the fixed current from M₁ pushes V_out **up** → positive (non‑inverting) gain.

**Input resistance (looking into the source):**
$$R_{in} = \frac{r_{o2}+r_{o1}}{1+G_{m2}r_{o2}} \approx \frac{1}{G_{m2}}\left(1+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o2}}\right)\quad(\text{low})$$

**Output resistance (looking into V_out, with input source resistance R_S):**
$$R_{out} = r_{o1}\,\Big\|\,\big[\,r_{o2} + (1+G_{m2}r_{o2})R_S\,\big]$$
For an ideal input source (R_S = 0): $R_{out}= r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$ (high).

## Key Characteristics / Uses
- **Non‑inverting** voltage gain ≈ $G_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$ — high because of the current‑source load.
- **Low input impedance** (~1/g_m) and **high output impedance** → behaves as a good **current buffer** (current follower).
- Gate is grounded ⟹ **no Miller multiplication of C_gd** ⟹ excellent high‑frequency response.
- Commonly used in **cascode stages, RF/LNA input stages, and current buffering**.

# Circuit Analysis

## Identification

This is a **common-gate (CG) amplifier** with an **active (current-source) load**.

| Device | Type | Terminals | Role |
|--------|------|-----------|------|
| **M₁** | PMOS | Source → V_DD, Gate → V_b2 (fixed), Drain → V_out | Current-source load (output resistance r_o1) |
| **M₂** | NMOS | Source → V_in, Gate → V_b1 (fixed), Drain → V_out | Common-gate amplifying transistor |

The defining feature: the **gate of M₂ is held at a DC bias (V_b1)**, so it is an AC ground. The **input is applied to the source**, and the **output is taken at the drain** — this is the common-gate topology.

## DC Biasing

Since M₁ and M₂ are in series, they carry the same current:

$$I_{D1} = I_{D2}$$

M₁ sets the bias current (gate–source voltage is fixed by V_DD − V_b2). For both transistors to stay in saturation:

$$V_{b1}-V_{THn} \le V_{out} \le V_{b2}+|V_{THp}|$$

## Small-Signal Analysis

Replacing M₁ with its output resistance r_o1 (VDD = AC ground) and writing KCL at the output node (gate at AC ground, source driven by V_in):

**Voltage gain (non-inverting):**

$$A_v = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{r_{o1}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}} \;\approx\; (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\,\|\,r_{o2})$$

> Note the **positive sign** — a common-gate stage does *not* invert.

**Input resistance (looking into the source of M₂):**

$$R_{in} = \frac{r_{o2}+r_{o1}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \text{ (for modest loads)}$$

→ **Low input impedance.**

**Output resistance (ideal input source, R_S = 0):**

$$R_{out} = r_{o2}\,\|\,r_{o1}$$

(With a source resistance R_S, the resistance looking into M₂'s drain rises to $r_{o2}[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_S]+R_S$.)

## Key Characteristics

- ✅ **Non-inverting** voltage gain  
- ✅ **Low input impedance** (≈ 1/g_m) → good as a **current buffer** (unity current gain, input current ≈ output current)  
- ✅ **No Miller multiplication** of the gate–drain capacitance → **excellent high-frequency response**  
- ✅ Body effect included via g_mb (M₂'s source sits above ground)

## Typical Applications

- The current-steering (top) device in a **cascode** amplifier  
- **Current buffer** / current follower  
- **RF low-noise amplifiers** where the low input impedance provides 50 Ω matching

# Circuit Analysis

## Topology Identification

This is a **common-gate (CG) amplifier** with an active (current-source) load.

| Device | Type | Terminals | Role |
|--------|------|-----------|------|
| $M_1$ | PMOS | S = $V_{DD}$, G = $V_{b2}$, D = $V_{out}$ | Current-source load |
| $M_2$ | NMOS | S = $V_{in}$, G = $V_{b1}$, D = $V_{out}$ | Common-gate gain device |

The signal enters at the **source** of $M_2$, the gate is held at a fixed bias $V_{b1}$ (AC ground), and the output is taken at the **drain** — the defining feature of a common-gate stage.

## DC Biasing

- $M_1$ is biased by $V_{b2}$ to deliver a constant current $I_D$; its drain-source resistance is $r_{o1}$.
- $V_{b1}$ sets $V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{in,DC}$; requires $V_{b1}-V_{in,DC}>V_{TH,n}$.
- **Saturation conditions:**
  - $M_2$: $V_{out}>V_{b1}-V_{TH,n}$
  - $M_1$: $V_{out}<V_{DD}-|V_{ov1}|$

## Small-Signal Analysis

Since $v_{gs1}=0$, $M_1$ appears simply as $r_{o1}$ to AC ground. Writing KCL at the output node (with $v_{gs2}=v_{bs2}=-v_{in}$):

$$-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}+\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}=0$$

**Voltage gain (non-inverting):**

→ **Low input impedance** (a few times $1/g_m$).

**Output resistance** (source driven by $R_S$):

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel\Big\{r_{o2}\big[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_S\big]+R_S\Big\}$$

With an ideal input source ($R_S=0$): $R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$.

## Key Properties

- ✅ **Non-inverting** gain (↑$V_{in}$ → ↓$I_{D2}$ → ↑$V_{out}$)
- ✅ **Low input / high output impedance** → acts as a **current buffer** (current gain ≈ 1)
- ✅ **No Miller multiplication** of $C_{gd}$ (gate grounded) → **excellent high-frequency response**

## Typical Applications
Cascode current buffers, RF low-noise amplifiers (for $50\,\Omega$ input matching via $R_{in}\approx 1/g_m$), and the upper half of folded/telescopic cascode structures.

# Circuit Analysis

## What the Circuit Is

This is an **inverting common‑source (CS) amplifier** built from two *stacked* NMOS transistors:

| Device | Source | Gate | Drain |
|--------|--------|------|-------|
| $M_1$ | ground | $V_{in}$ | node X |
| $M_2$ | node X | $V_{in}$ | $V_{out}$ |

$R_D$ ties $V_{DD}$ to the drain of $M_2$ (the output). Because the two transistors are in series **and share the same gate node**, this is a **self‑cascode** structure — *not* a true cascode (a true cascode would hold $M_2$'s gate at a fixed bias).

## DC Operating Point

The same current $I_D$ flows through both devices, and

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in}, \qquad V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_X \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; V_{GS2}<V_{GS1}.$$

For $M_1$ to be saturated we'd need $V_X \ge V_{in}-V_{TH1}$; for $M_2$ to be saturated we need $V_X \le V_{in}-V_{TH2}$. Since $M_2$ suffers **body effect** ($V_{SB2}=V_X>0 \Rightarrow V_{TH2}>V_{TH1}$), these cannot both hold.

> **Result:** $M_1$ is *forced into the triode region*; $M_2$ operates in *saturation*. $M_1$ behaves like a small voltage‑controlled resistor $R_{on1}=1/g_{ds1}$, and $V_X$ settles to equalize the two currents. (For identical devices, $V_X\approx 0.29\,(V_{in}-V_{TH})$.)

## Small‑Signal Gain

Using $g_{m1}, g_{ds1}$ for $M_1$ (triode) and $g_{m2}$ for $M_2$ (saturation), KCL at node X ($i_{d1}=i_{d2}$) and at the output ($i_{d2}=-v_{out}/R_D$) give the composite transconductance:

$$G_m=\frac{i_{out}}{v_{in}}=g_{m2}\,\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}}$$

$$A_v=-G_m\,(R_D\,\|\,R_{out})\;\approx\;-\,g_{m2}R_D\cdot\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}}$$

Since $M_1$ is in triode, $g_{ds1}$ is large ($g_{ds1}\gg g_{m1},g_{m2}$), so node X is pinned near AC ground and

$$\boxed{A_v \approx -\,g_{m2}R_D}$$

$M_2$ acts as the signal device. (For *identical* transistors the exact factor gives $G_m\approx0.5\,k(V_{in}-V_{TH})\approx0.7\,g_{m2}$.)

## Impedances

- **Input:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (into the gates at low frequency).
- **Output** ($v_{in}=0$): $M_2$ cascodes the triode resistance of $M_1$,
$$R_{out}\approx r_{o2}\,(1+g_{m2}R_{on1})+R_{on1}\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}R_{on1},$$
i.e. higher than a single device — the "self‑cascode" benefit — but since $R_D\ll R_{out}$ the gain is still set by $R_D$.

## Key Takeaways

- Functionally it is an **inverting CS amplifier**, $|A_v|\approx g_{m2}R_D$.
- Tying $M_2$'s gate to the input (rather than a fixed bias) means this is **not a gain‑boosting cascode** — the stacked device mainly raises output impedance, while costing an extra $V_{DS}$ of headroom (smaller output swing) and a somewhat reduced effective transconductance.
- $M_1$ always lives in **triode**; $M_2$ carries the signal in **saturation**.

# Circuit Analysis

## Topology

This is a **common‑source (CS) amplifier** in which the single input transistor has been replaced by **two stacked NMOS devices in series, both driven by the same input**:

- $M_1$: bottom device, source at ground, gate at $V_{in}$
- $M_2$: top device, source at the internal node $V_X$, gate at $V_{in}$, drain at $V_{out}$
- $R_D$: load resistor from $V_{DD}$ to the output node

Since the two transistors are in series, **they carry the same drain current** $I_D$.

## Key result: $M_1$ is always in triode

Let $V_X$ be the voltage at the node between the devices.

- For $M_2$ to conduct, it needs $V_{GS2} = V_{in}-V_X > V_{TH}$, i.e.
$$V_X < V_{in}-V_{TH}$$
- For $M_1$ to be in **saturation**, it would need $V_{DS1}=V_X \ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$.

These two conditions are contradictory. Therefore, whenever current flows:

$$\boxed{M_1 \text{ operates in the triode region, } M_2 \text{ in saturation}}$$

## Equivalent single transistor

Equating $M_1$'s triode current to $M_2$'s saturation current (using $V_{ov1}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$, $V_{ov2}=V_{in}-V_X-V_{TH}$):

$$\underbrace{\tfrac{k_1}{2}\left(V_{ov1}^2-V_{ov2}^2\right)}_{M_1,\ \text{triode}}=\underbrace{\tfrac{k_2}{2}V_{ov2}^2}_{M_2,\ \text{sat}}
\;\Rightarrow\; V_{ov2}^2=\frac{k_1}{k_1+k_2}\,V_{ov1}^2$$

Substituting back gives a clean result:

$$\boxed{I_D=\tfrac12\,k_{eq}\,(V_{in}-V_{TH})^2,\qquad k_{eq}=\frac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}}$$

where $k_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$. 

**Interpretation:** $\dfrac{1}{k_{eq}}=\dfrac{1}{k_1}+\dfrac{1}{k_2}$ — exactly like channel lengths adding in series. The pair behaves as **one longer‑channel NMOS** with overdrive $V_{in}-V_{TH}$.

## Transfer characteristic and gain

While $M_2$ stays saturated:

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-\tfrac12\,k_{eq}(V_{in}-V_{TH})^2\,R_D$$

$$\boxed{A_v=\frac{dV_{out}}{dV_{in}}=-\,k_{eq}(V_{in}-V_{TH})\,R_D=-\frac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}(V_{in}-V_{TH})\,R_D}$$

**Identical devices** $(k_1=k_2=k)$:

$$A_v=-\tfrac12\,k(V_{in}-V_{TH})R_D,\quad I_D=\tfrac14 k(V_{in}-V_{TH})^2,\quad V_X\approx0.29(V_{in}-V_{TH})$$

## Validity conditions

| Region | Condition | Behavior |
|--------|-----------|----------|
| Off | $V_{in}<V_{TH}$ | $V_{out}=V_{DD}$ |
| Active (amplifier) | $V_{out}>V_{in}-V_{TH}$ | linear gain above |
| Both triode | $V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{TH}$ | output pulled low (overdriven) |

## Practical notes

- **Body effect:** $M_2$ has $V_{SB2}=V_X>0$, raising $V_{TH2}$ and slightly lowering $I_D$ and gain.
- **Channel‑length modulation:** adds finite $r_o$; to first order $R_{out}\approx R_D$.
- **Bottom line:** stacking two common‑gate devices gives *lower* $G_m$ and current than a single device of size $k_1$ — it is equivalent to using a weaker/longer transistor, not a technique for boosting gain.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate-driven series NMOS pair, places M1 in triode and M2 in saturation, and derives the equivalent longer-channel device. The imprecise region boundaries and final “common-gate devices” wording are secondary to the correct central result.

## Circuit Identification

This is a **common‑source (CS) amplifier** built from two stacked NMOS transistors with a drain resistor $R_D$:

- $M_1$ – driver, source grounded, drain at internal node $X$
- $M_2$ – stacked on top, source at $X$, drain at $V_{out}$
- **Both gates are tied to $V_{in}$**
- Output taken at the drain of $M_2$; load = $R_D$ to $V_{DD}$

It is an **inverting voltage amplifier** with $R_{in}=\infty$ (MOS gates).

## Terminal Voltages and the Key Insight

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in},\qquad V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_X$$

Both devices carry the **same current** $I_D$ (series), and $V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_DR_D$.

Notice $V_{GS1}>V_{GS2}$ (since $V_X>0$), yet both pass equal current. **This forces $M_1$ into the triode region.** Proof: if both were saturated,

$$k_1V_{ov1}^2=k_2V_{ov2}^2,\quad V_{ov2}=V_{ov1}-V_X\le V_{ov1}$$

but $M_1$ saturation requires $V_X\ge V_{ov1}$, i.e. $V_{ov2}\le 0$ ($M_2$ off) — a contradiction.

$$\boxed{M_1 \text{ in triode},\qquad M_2 \text{ in saturation}}$$

So $M_1$ acts as a voltage‑controlled **resistor** and $M_2$ is the real amplifying device (degenerated by $M_1$). Here $k_i\equiv\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$.

## Bias Equations

$$I_D=\tfrac12 k_2\,(V_{in}-V_X-V_{TH})^2\quad(M_2\text{ sat})$$
$$I_D=k_1\!\left[(V_{in}-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12 V_X^2\right]\quad(M_1\text{ triode})$$

## Small‑Signal Gain

Small‑signal analysis (neglecting channel‑length modulation) gives

$$A_v=-g_{m2}R_D\,\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}}$$

Using the triode identities $g_{m1}+g_{ds1}=k_1V_{ov1}$, $\;g_{ds1}=k_1V_{ov2}$, $\;g_{m2}=k_2V_{ov2}$, the node voltage cancels and the result is remarkably clean:

$$\boxed{G_m=\frac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}\,(V_{in}-V_{TH}),\qquad A_v=-\frac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}\,(V_{in}-V_{TH})\,R_D}$$

**Intuition (deep triode):** $M_1\approx R_{on1}=\dfrac{1}{k_1(V_{in}-V_{TH})}$, and because $g_{m1}=k_1V_X\!\approx\!0$ its own gate drive is ineffective — so the circuit reduces to a *source‑degenerated* CS stage:

$$A_v\approx-\frac{g_{m2}R_D}{1+g_{m2}R_{on1}}$$

## Other Quantities

- **Output resistance:** $R_{out}=R_D\parallel\big[r_{o2}(1+g_{m2}R_{on1})+R_{on1}\big]\approx R_D$
- **Output swing:** $M_2$ stays saturated while $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{TH}$
- **Identical devices** ($k_1=k_2=k$): $\;G_m=\tfrac12 k(V_{in}-V_{TH})=\tfrac12 g_{m,\text{single}}$. The stack behaves like **one transistor of double the channel length** (at equal current, $G_m=g_m/\sqrt2$).

## Takeaway

Tying the upper transistor's gate to the **input** (instead of to a fixed DC bias) does **not** produce a high‑gain cascode. Instead $M_1$ is driven into triode, and the stage behaves like a common‑source amplifier with a **reduced effective transconductance** $G_m=\dfrac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}(V_{in}-V_{TH})$ — always smaller than that of either single transistor alone.

The extra small-signal analysis is consistent with that equivalent-channel result; its simplifying intuition does not change the essential answer.

# Circuit Analysis

## Identifying the Topology

Let me label the common source node (where the two sources and $I_1$ meet) as node **P**.

Looking at each transistor's role:

| Transistor | Gate | Drain | Source | Function |
|------------|------|-------|--------|----------|
| $M_1$ | $V_{in}$ (signal) | $V_{DD}$ (AC gnd) | node P | **Source follower** (common-drain) |
| $M_2$ | $V_b$ (fixed → AC gnd) | $V_{out}$ via $R_D$ | node P | **Common-gate** amplifier |

So this is a **source-follower ($M_1$) driving a common-gate stage ($M_2$)** — equivalently, a **differential pair driven single-endedly** ($V_{in}$ on one gate, $V_b$ fixed on the other) with the output taken from only one drain.

## DC Operating Point

The tail source fixes the total current:
$$I_{D1} + I_{D2} = I_1, \qquad V_{out} = V_{DD} - I_{D2}R_D$$

The DC levels of $V_{in}$ and $V_b$ set the current split. For matched devices with $V_{in,DC} = V_b$, the current divides equally: $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1/2$. ($M_1$ is easily in saturation since its drain sits at $V_{DD}$.)

## Qualitative Operation (sign)

$$V_{in}\!\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; V_P\!\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; V_{GS2}=V_b-V_P\!\downarrow \;\Rightarrow\; I_{D2}\!\downarrow \;\Rightarrow\; V_{out}\!\uparrow$$

**→ This is a *non-inverting* amplifier.**

## Small-Signal Gain

Treat $I_1$ as ideal (its AC current = 0), so the two drain currents sum to zero at node P. Neglecting $r_o$:

$$\underbrace{g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_P)}_{i_{d1}} \;\underbrace{-\,g_{m2}v_P}_{i_{d2}} = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; v_P = \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,v_{in}$$

The output is produced by the common-gate device:
$$v_{out} = -i_{d2}R_D = g_{m2}R_D\,v_P$$

$$\boxed{A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{g_{m1}\,g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,R_D}$$

**For matched transistors** ($g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m$):
$$A_v = \frac{g_m R_D}{2} \quad (\text{positive})$$

*Interpretation:* source-follower gain $\dfrac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}$ (follower loaded by $1/g_{m2}$) × common-gate gain $g_{m2}R_D$.

## Input / Output Impedance

- **Input:** $R_{in} = \infty$ (looking into the gate of $M_1$).
- **Output:** looking into $M_2$'s drain (common-gate with source degeneration $R_P\approx 1/g_{m1}$):
$$R_{out} = R_D \,\|\, \big[r_{o2}(1+g_{m2}R_P)+R_P\big] \;\approx\; R_D \,\|\, 2r_{o2} \;\approx\; R_D$$

## Key Takeaways

- The stage gives **non-inverting** gain of $\tfrac{1}{2}g_mR_D$ — exactly **half** that of a plain common-source stage, but with the opposite (non-inverting) polarity and a **high input impedance**.
- Useful as a non-inverting / level-shifting gain stage.

*(Including body effect replaces $g_{m2}$ with $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$, etc.; including channel-length modulation modifies the result only slightly when $R_D \ll r_o$.)*

# Circuit Analysis

## Topology Identification

This is a **two‑stage compound amplifier** that can be read two equivalent ways:

- **$M_1$** → **source follower (common‑drain):** its gate is the input $V_{in}$, its drain ties directly to $V_{DD}$ (AC ground), so no gain is produced at its drain; the signal appears at its **source**.
- **$M_2$** → **common‑gate stage:** its gate sits at the fixed bias $V_b$ (AC ground), its **source** is the common node driven by $M_1$, and its drain develops $V_{out}$ across $R_D$.

Equivalently, this is a **differential pair** ($M_1,M_2$ sharing tail source $I_1$) driven single‑endedly at $V_{in}$, with the output taken single‑endedly at $M_2$'s drain.

**Signal path:** $V_{in} \to$ gate $M_1 \to$ common source node $\to$ drain $M_2 \to V_{out}$

## DC Operating Point

The tail current splits between the two devices:
$$I_{D1} + I_{D2} = I_1, \qquad V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D$$
(Both $M_1$ and $M_2$ must remain in saturation.)

## Small‑Signal Gain

Set $V_{DD}, V_b \to$ AC ground; the ideal current source $I_1$ is an **AC open**. Let $v_X$ be the common‑source node.

**KCL at node $X$** (sum of the two source currents = 0):
$$g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_X) - g_{m2}v_X = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \boxed{v_X=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,v_{in}}$$

This is just the follower gain loaded by $M_2$'s input resistance $1/g_{m2}$.

**Output node** — the current through $R_D$ equals $M_2$'s drain current:
$$v_{out}=-i_{d2}R_D=g_{m2}R_D\,v_X$$

Combining:
$$\boxed{A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}\,g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,R_D \;>0 \text{ (non-inverting)}}$$

For matched devices $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m$:
$$A_v=\frac{g_m R_D}{2}$$

> **Note the sign:** unlike a common‑source stage, this amplifier is **non‑inverting** — a follower (non‑inverting) in series with a common‑gate stage (non‑inverting). The price for this is a gain of only ~half that of a plain common‑source stage, because the follower attenuates by $g_{m1}/(g_{m1}+g_{m2})$.

## Input / Output Impedance

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| $R_{in}$ | $\infty$ (gate of $M_1$) |
| $R_{out}$ | $\approx R_D$ (ignoring $r_o$) |

*(With finite $r_o$, $M_2$ acts as a cascode-like device so the resistance looking into its drain is large, and $R_{out}\approx R_D$ still holds; the gain expression gets small correction factors.)*

## Summary
A high‑input‑impedance, **non‑inverting** amplifier formed by a source follower ($M_1$) driving a common‑gate stage ($M_2$), with gain $\dfrac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_D}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}$ (= $g_mR_D/2$ when matched).

This is a **source-coupled (differential) pair driven single-endedly**:

| Device | Gate | Drain | Source |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| $M_1$ | $V_{in}$ (signal) | $V_{DD}$ directly | common node $P$ |

**Signal-flow interpretation:** $M_1$ acts as a **source follower** (common-drain, since its drain is at AC ground) and $M_2$ acts as a **common-gate** stage (its gate is an AC ground). So the path is:

$$V_{in} \xrightarrow{\text{source follower } M_1} V_P \xrightarrow{\text{common gate } M_2} V_{out}$$

## DC Bias

$$I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_1,\qquad V_P = V_{in,DC}-V_{GS1}=V_b-V_{GS2},\qquad V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D$$

With matched devices and $V_{in,DC}=V_b$, the current splits evenly: $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1/2$. ($M_1$ is always in saturation since its drain sits at $V_{DD}$; $M_2$ needs $V_{out}-V_P \ge V_{ov2}$.)

## Small-Signal Gain

Let $v_P$ be the common-source node. Writing the drain currents (neglecting $r_o$):

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_P),\qquad i_{d2}=g_{m2}(0-v_P)=-g_{m2}v_P$$

Since the ideal tail source carries no AC current, **KCL at node P** gives $i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$:

$$g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_P)-g_{m2}v_P=0\ \Rightarrow\ v_P=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,v_{in}$$

The output is taken at $M_2$'s drain, $v_{out}=-i_{d2}R_D=g_{m2}v_P R_D$:

$$\boxed{\;\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,R_D\;\xrightarrow{g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m}\;+\frac{g_mR_D}{2}\;}$$

**The gain is non-inverting.** Intuitively: $v_{in}\uparrow \Rightarrow I_{D1}\uparrow \Rightarrow I_{D2}=I_1-I_{D1}\downarrow \Rightarrow$ smaller drop across $R_D \Rightarrow V_{out}\uparrow$.

## Impedances

- **Input:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (gate of $M_1$).
- **Output:** $R_{out}=R_D\parallel R_{out,M2}$. Looking into $M_2$'s drain (degenerated by $\approx 1/g_{m1}$ at its source) gives $R_{out,M2}\approx 2r_{o2}$, so $R_{out}\approx R_D$ when $R_D\ll r_o$.

## Summary

- **Function:** Non-inverting amplifier with voltage gain $\tfrac{1}{2}g_mR_D$ (half that of a common-source stage, because the source-follower front end loses a factor of 2).
- **Key advantages:** high input impedance, and—being a cascade of common-drain + common-gate—**no Miller multiplication of $C_{gd}$**, giving wide bandwidth.

## Identifying the Circuit

This is a **source follower**:

- **M₁** is the follower (drain at $V_{DD}$, source at $V_{out}$), with a resistor $R_S$ in series with its gate.
- **M₂** (gate at fixed bias $V_b$) is just a current‑source load/bias element. For small signals its gate and source are grounded, so it contributes only its large output resistance $r_{o2}$ in parallel — it plays **no role** in the inductive effect.

So the behavior is set entirely by M₁, its $g_m$, its gate–source capacitance $C_{gs}$, and $R_S$.

## Small‑Signal Output Impedance

Ground $V_{in}$, apply a test voltage $V_x$ at the output (source), and find $I_x$. (Neglecting $r_o$, $C_{gd}$, body effect.)

**Gate‑node KCL** — the only current into the gate comes through $C_{gs}$ and leaves through $R_S$:

$$(V_x - V_G)sC_{gs} = \frac{V_G}{R_S} \;\Rightarrow\; V_G = \frac{sR_SC_{gs}}{1+sR_SC_{gs}}\,V_x$$

so

$$V_{gs}=V_G-V_x=\frac{-V_x}{1+sR_SC_{gs}}$$

**Source‑node KCL:**

$$I_x = (V_x-V_G)sC_{gs} - g_m V_{gs} = \frac{(g_m + sC_{gs})}{1+sR_SC_{gs}}\,V_x$$

$$\boxed{Z_{out}(s) = \frac{1 + sR_SC_{gs}}{\,g_m + sC_{gs}\,}}$$

## Why It's Inductive

**Limiting values:**

$$Z_{out}(0)=\frac{1}{g_m}, \qquad Z_{out}(\infty)=R_S$$

Setting $s=j\omega$:

$$\operatorname{Im}\{Z_{out}\}=\frac{\omega C_{gs}\,(g_mR_S-1)}{g_m^2+\omega^2C_{gs}^2}$$

This is **positive (inductive)** whenever

$$\boxed{R_S > \tfrac{1}{g_m}}$$

Then the magnitude *rises* with frequency (from $1/g_m$ up toward $R_S$), the hallmark of an inductor.

**Exact equivalent network:**

$$Z_{out}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{g_m}}_{\text{DC }R} \;+\; \Big[\,(R_S-\tfrac{1}{g_m})\;\|\;sL\,\Big],\qquad L=\frac{C_{gs}}{g_m}\left(R_S-\frac{1}{g_m}\right)$$

The inductance $L$ is positive only when $R_S>1/g_m$ — the same condition.

## Physical Intuition

The ideal follower corrects its output strongly, giving low impedance $1/g_m$. The gate resistance introduces a **delay** in how the gate can respond:

- **Low frequency:** $C_{gs}$ is open; the gate stays at its DC value, so a change in $V_{out}$ fully appears as $V_{gs}$. The transistor reacts strongly → low impedance $1/g_m$.
- **High frequency:** $C_{gs}$ couples the source swing up to the gate faster than $R_S$ can "reset" it, so the gate rides along with the source. $V_{gs}$ barely changes, the transistor hardly reacts → high impedance ($\to R_S$).

Impedance that **increases with frequency** = inductive. Equivalently, the output current lags the voltage, i.e. a positive (inductive) phase.

## Practical Consequence

This inductive output impedance resonates with any **load capacitance** $C_L$, forming an $RLC$ network. This causes **frequency‑response peaking and step‑response ringing**, and with insufficient damping a source follower can even **oscillate** — a well‑known reason to keep the gate‑drive resistance small.

## Circuit Identification

- **M₁** is a **source follower** (common‑drain): drain to $V_{DD}$, gate driven from $V_{in}$ through the series resistance $R_S$, source = $V_{out}$.
- **M₂** (gate at $V_b$) is a **current‑source load**, presenting a high impedance at the output.

So the output impedance is essentially what we see **looking into the source of M₁**, with a resistor $R_S$ in series with its gate.

## Small‑Signal Derivation

Set $V_{in}=0$ (so the gate sees $R_S$ to AC ground), let the drain be AC ground, keep only $C_{gs}$, and apply a test source $V_x,\,I_x$ at the output.

**Gate node KCL** (only $R_S$ and $C_{gs}$ attach here):

$$(V_x-V_g)\,sC_{gs}=\frac{V_g}{R_S}\;\Rightarrow\; V_g=\frac{sR_SC_{gs}}{1+sR_SC_{gs}}\,V_x$$

so that

$$V_{gs}=V_g-V_x=\frac{-V_x}{1+sR_SC_{gs}}$$

**Output node KCL** $\;I_x=\dfrac{V_g}{R_S}-g_mV_{gs}$ gives

$$\boxed{Z_{out}(s)=\frac{V_x}{I_x}=\frac{1+sR_SC_{gs}}{g_m+sC_{gs}}}$$

## Why This Is Inductive

Look at the two limits:

$$Z_{out}(0)=\frac{1}{g_m}\qquad\qquad Z_{out}(\infty)=R_S$$

The impedance **rises from $1/g_m$ to $R_S$** as frequency increases. An impedance magnitude that *grows* with frequency is the signature of an inductor.

Make it quantitative — substitute $s=j\omega$:

$$\operatorname{Im}\{Z_{out}\}=\frac{\omega C_{gs}\,(g_mR_S-1)}{g_m^{2}+\omega^{2}C_{gs}^{2}}$$

This is **positive (inductive) whenever**

$$\boxed{R_S>\frac{1}{g_m}}$$

### Equivalent RL network
Rewriting $Z_{out}$ as an admittance,

$$Y_{out}=\frac{1}{R_S}+\frac{1}{R_2+sL_2},\qquad R_2=\frac{R_S}{g_mR_S-1},\quad L_2=\frac{R_S^{2}C_{gs}}{g_mR_S-1}$$

i.e. $R_S$ **in parallel with a series $R$–$L$ branch**. The equivalent inductance $L_2$ is positive only when $g_mR_S>1$, exactly the condition above.

## Physical Picture

- At **low frequency** $C_{gs}$ is open; the gate is held at AC ground and the transistor behaves like a resistor $1/g_m$ (the normal follower output).
- At **high frequency** $C_{gs}$ shorts the gate to the source, so $V_{gs}\to 0$ and the device **stops conducting the controlling current $g_mV_{gs}$**. The only remaining path for the test current is through $C_{gs}$ and $R_S$, giving $Z_{out}\to R_S$.

Thus the low impedance produced by the $g_m$ feedback is **progressively disabled** as frequency rises. Equivalently, the $R_SC_{gs}$ network **delays** the gate voltage, so the transistor's corrective current **lags** the output voltage — and a current lagging the voltage is precisely what an inductor does.

## Practical Consequence

Because the follower output looks inductive, when it drives a capacitive load $C_L$ (including M₂'s junction capacitances) it forms an **LC tank**. This causes frequency‑response **peaking, step‑response ringing, and potential instability** — the well‑known reason source followers must be used with care when $R_S$ is large.

## Circuit Identification

This is a **source follower**: $M_1$ is the follower (drain to $V_{DD}$, gate driven through $R_S$, source = output), and $M_2$ is a current‑source load setting the bias current. The output impedance is what you see **looking into the source of $M_1$**.

Normally a follower has a low, purely resistive output resistance of $1/g_m$. The series gate resistance $R_S$, acting together with $C_{gs}$, is what introduces the inductive behavior.

## Small‑Signal Derivation

Neglect $r_o$, body effect, and $C_{gd}$ for clarity (they change details, not the essential result). Apply a test voltage $v_x$ at the output (source) and find $i_x$. The gate node $v_g$ connects to AC ground through $R_S$, with $C_{gs}$ to the source.

**KCL at the gate:**
$$\frac{v_g}{R_S} + (v_g - v_x)sC_{gs} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_g = v_x\,\frac{sR_S C_{gs}}{1+sR_S C_{gs}}$$

**KCL at the source:**
$$i_x + g_m v_{gs} = (v_x - v_g)sC_{gs}, \qquad v_{gs}=v_g-v_x$$
$$i_x = (v_x - v_g)(g_m + sC_{gs})$$

Since $v_x - v_g = \dfrac{v_x}{1+sR_S C_{gs}}$:

$$\boxed{Z_{out}(s) = \frac{v_x}{i_x} = \frac{1 + sR_S C_{gs}}{g_m + sC_{gs}}}$$

## Why This Is Inductive

**Frequency limits:**
$$Z_{out}(0) = \frac{1}{g_m}, \qquad Z_{out}(\infty) = R_S$$

If $R_S > 1/g_m$, the magnitude **rises** with frequency — the hallmark of an inductor. The zero $(1/R_SC_{gs})$ sits below the pole $(g_m/C_{gs})$, and in between $|Z|$ climbs.

**Checking the reactance:**
$$\operatorname{Im}\{Z_{out}(j\omega)\} = \frac{\omega C_{gs}\,(g_m R_S - 1)}{g_m^2 + \omega^2 C_{gs}^2}$$

This is **positive (inductive) whenever $g_m R_S > 1$.**

**Equivalent network** (valid for $g_m R_S>1$): a resistor in series with a parallel R–L,

$$R_1 = \frac{1}{g_m},\quad R_2 = R_S-\frac{1}{g_m},\quad L = \left(R_S-\frac{1}{g_m}\right)\frac{C_{gs}}{g_m}$$

## Physical Intuition

A follower keeps its output impedance low through local feedback: pushing the source up reduces $v_{GS}$, which cuts the drain current and opposes the change. **This feedback requires the gate to be held fixed.**

- At **low frequency**, $C_{gs}$ is open and $R_S$ holds the gate steady → full feedback → $Z_{out}=1/g_m$.
- At **high frequency**, $C_{gs}$ couples the source perturbation onto the gate. Because $R_S$ no longer holds the gate firmly, the gate partially *follows* the source, so $v_{GS}$ changes less, the current feedback weakens, and the impedance rises toward $R_S$.

An impedance that increases with frequency = positive reactance = **inductive**.

## Practical Note

This inductive output impedance can resonate with a capacitive load $C_L$, producing **peaking in the frequency response and ringing in the step response**, a well‑known hazard for source followers driving capacitive loads from a resistive (high‑$R_S$) source.

# Circuit Analysis

## Topology Identification

Let me first identify what each device does:

| Device | Gate | Drain | Source | Role |
|--------|------|-------|--------|------|
| $M_1$ | node $X$ | $V_{out}$ | GND | Common‑source gain stage (load $R_{D1}$) |
| $M_2$ | $V_{out}$ | node $X$ | GND | Feedback device (senses $V_{out}$, returns current to $X$) |

The input is a **current** $I_{in}$ injected into node $X$, and the output is the **voltage** $V_{out}$. This is a **transimpedance (current‑in / voltage‑out) configuration with feedback** — two cascaded common‑source stages forming a loop ($X \to V_{out} \to X$).

## DC Operating Point

Since the gate of $M_1$ draws no current, **all of $I_{in}$ must flow into the drain of $M_2$** (KCL at $X$):

$$\boxed{I_{D2} = I_{in}}$$

This fixes $V_{out}$, because $V_{out}=V_{GS2}$ must be whatever value makes $M_2$ carry $I_{in}$:

$$V_{out}=V_{TH2}+\sqrt{\dfrac{2I_{in}}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_2}}$$

Then $M_1$ supplies the current demanded by the resistor, setting $V_X$:

$$I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}},\qquad V_X=V_{GS1}(I_{D1})$$

## Small‑Signal Transimpedance

**Node $V_{out}$** (current through $R_{D1}$ = $M_1$ drain current):
$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D1}} = g_{m1}v_x \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; v_x=-\frac{v_{out}}{g_{m1}R_{D1}}$$

**Node $X$** ($I_{in}$ flows entirely into $M_2$):
$$i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{out}\;\;\Rightarrow\;\; v_{out}=\frac{i_{in}}{g_{m2}}$$

$$\boxed{\dfrac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} \approx \dfrac{1}{g_{m2}}}$$

(Including channel‑length modulation: $\dfrac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=\dfrac{1}{g_{m2}-\frac{1}{g_{m1}R_1 r_{o2}}}\approx\dfrac{1}{g_{m2}}$, with $R_1=R_{D1}\|r_{o1}$.)

**Key insight:** the gain is set *entirely by $M_2$* — independent of $M_1$ and $R_{D1}$. Because $M_2$ is forced to carry $I_{in}$, the output behaves like the gate of a diode‑connected device: $v_{out}=i_{in}/g_{m2}$.

## Input Resistance at Node X

$$R_{in,X}=\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}R_{D1}}\cdot\frac{1}{g_{m2}}=\boxed{-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}}$$

**This is negative** — pushing *more* current into $X$ makes $V_X$ *drop*.

## Feedback Polarity and Stability (important caveat)

Trace a perturbation: $v_x\!\uparrow \Rightarrow I_{D1}\!\uparrow \Rightarrow V_{out}\!\downarrow \Rightarrow I_{D2}\!\downarrow$. With $I_{in}$ fixed, the excess current charges node $X$, so $v_x\!\uparrow$ *even more*.

Both stages invert, so the loop gain is **positive**:
$$T=\underbrace{(g_{m1}R_1)}_{M_1}\underbrace{(g_{m2}r_{o2})}_{M_2}>0,\qquad T\gg 1$$

The dynamic system matrix has a **negative determinant** ($\propto \tfrac{1}{R_1 r_{o2}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}<0$), giving a right‑half‑plane pole.

**Conclusion:** this is a **regenerative (positive‑feedback) loop**. The negative input resistance confirms it. The transimpedance $1/g_{m2}$ and the small‑signal numbers above describe an **unstable equilibrium** — in practice the circuit latches to a rail rather than acting as a well‑behaved transimpedance amplifier. (To make this a usable amplifier, the feedback sense would have to be inverted, e.g., by adding a third inversion in the loop.)

# Circuit Analysis

Reading the connections:

| Device | Gate | Drain | Source |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| **M₁** | node X (input) | V_out | ground |
| **M₂** | V_out | node X | ground |

- **M₁** is a **common‑source stage** with load $R_{D1}$ (input at X, output at V_out).
- **M₂** is a **feedback device**: it *senses* V_out at its gate and *returns current* to node X through its drain.
- The input is a current $I_{in}$ injected into node X.

This is a **shunt‑shunt feedback loop** (current in, voltage out).

## Feedback Polarity

Trace a disturbance around the loop:

$$v_X\uparrow \;\xrightarrow{M_1\,(\text{inverting})}\; v_{out}\downarrow \;\xrightarrow{\;M_2\text{ gate}\;}\; I_{D2}\downarrow \;\Rightarrow\; \text{less current pulled from X} \;\Rightarrow\; v_X\uparrow$$

➡️ **This is POSITIVE (regenerative) feedback.**

## DC Operating Point

Node X draws no DC gate current, so **all of** $I_{in}$ must flow into M₂'s drain:

$$\boxed{I_{D2}=I_{in}}$$

Since $I_{D2}$ is controlled by $V_{GS2}=V_{out}$:

$$V_{out}=V_{TH}+\sqrt{\dfrac{2I_{in}}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_2}}$$

Then $I_{D1}=\dfrac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}$ sets $V_X=V_{TH}+\sqrt{2I_{D1}/[\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1]}$.

## Small‑Signal Analysis

Let $R_1 = R_{D1}\|r_{o1}$. Nodal equations:

$$\text{(out):}\quad v_{out}=-g_{m1}R_1\,v_X \qquad\qquad \text{(X):}\quad i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{out}+\frac{v_X}{r_{o2}}$$

**Transimpedance gain** (dominated by the feedback element M₂):

$$\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}R_1r_{o2}}\,}\;\;\approx\;\;\boxed{\dfrac{1}{g_{m2}}}$$

The loop forces M₂ to carry $i_{in}$, so $v_{out}$ simply tracks the required $V_{GS2}$.

**Input resistance at node X:**

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_X}{i_{in}}=\frac{r_{o2}}{\,1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1r_{o2}\,}\;\;\approx\;\;\boxed{-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1}}$$

Note the form $R_{in}=\dfrac{r_{o2}}{1-T}$ with loop gain $T=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1r_{o2}$ — the $(1-T)$ confirms positive feedback (negative feedback would give $1+T$).

## Key Conclusions

- **It behaves as a transimpedance converter** with $v_{out}/i_{in}\approx 1/g_{m2}$.
- Because the feedback is **positive**, the small‑signal input (and output) resistance is **negative**.
- With a realistic loop gain $T=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1r_{o2}>1$, the bias point is a regenerative/unstable one — driven from an ideal current source the node tends to **latch** rather than settle.

> ⚠️ To make this a *stable* transimpedance amplifier of value $1/g_{m2}$, the loop would need one additional inversion (so that rising $v_X$ causes M₂ to pull *more* current from X, i.e. negative feedback).

$$\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} = \frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\Vert r_{o1})}\,}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

$$R_{X}=\frac{v_X}{i_{in}} \approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}\,(R_{D1}\Vert r_{o1})}$$

Trace the loop:

$$v_X\!\uparrow \;\xrightarrow{M_1}\; v_{out}\!\downarrow \;\xrightarrow{M_2}\; I_{D2}\!\downarrow \;\Rightarrow\; M_2 \text{ pulls less from X} \;\Rightarrow\; v_X\!\uparrow \text{ (reinforced)}$$
